directAnswer: St. Zosimus was pope for less than two years, from 417 to 418, and is described in early sources as Greek. He reopened the case of Pelagius and Caelestius, at first criticizing the African bishops who had condemned them, but in 418 he issued a formal letter condemning Pelagianism. His reign was also marked by disputes with the African church and with bishops in Gaul.

paras: Zosimus succeeded Innocent I in March 417, only days after Innocent had confirmed the condemnation of Pelagius and his disciple Caelestius. Caelestius promptly came to Rome to plead his case in person, and Pelagius sent a statement of faith.

Impressed by their professions of loyalty, Zosimus wrote to the African bishops suggesting they had acted too hastily, and he gave them time to present clearer evidence. The Africans, led by Aurelius of Carthage and supported by Augustine, responded firmly that Innocent's judgment should stand.

In the spring of 418, a large council at Carthage restated the Church's teaching on original sin and grace, and Emperor Honorius ordered the expulsion of the Pelagian leaders from Rome. Zosimus, after further examination, issued a lengthy circular letter known as the Epistola Tractoria, which condemned Pelagius and Caelestius and required bishops to subscribe to it.

Most bishops did so. A group of Italian bishops led by Julian of Eclanum refused and were deposed. Julian went on to become Augustine's most persistent opponent in writing. The Tractoria survives only in fragments, but it marked the decisive papal rejection of Pelagianism.

sections.h2: Apiarius and the Bishops of Gaul
paras: Zosimus also clashed with Africa over Apiarius, a priest of Sicca deposed by his bishop who appealed to Rome. Zosimus supported the appeal, citing canons he believed came from Nicaea. The African bishops could not find them in their copies of the Nicene canons; they were in fact canons of the Council of Serdica. The dispute dragged on into the next two pontificates.

In Gaul, he granted Bishop Patroclus of Arles sweeping metropolitan rights and made him his representative there. This angered neighboring bishops and was largely undone by later popes. Facing opposition even among his own clergy, Zosimus fell ill and died on December 26, 418. He was buried in the basilica of St. Lawrence Outside the Walls.

keyFacts: Pope from March 417 to December 418; described as Greek by birth
Reopened and then confirmed the condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius
Issued the Epistola Tractoria against Pelagianism in 418
Disputed with African bishops over the appeal of the priest Apiarius
Buried at St. Lawrence Outside the Walls; feast day December 27

faqs.question: Did Pope Zosimus support Pelagius?
faqs.answer: Initially he was persuaded by the professions of faith from Pelagius and Caelestius and asked the African bishops to reconsider. After further evidence and a council at Carthage in 418, he condemned them in the Epistola Tractoria.

faqs.question: What was the Apiarius affair?
faqs.answer: Apiarius was an African priest who appealed his deposition to Rome. Zosimus backed the appeal using canons he attributed to Nicaea, which were actually from Serdica, causing a long dispute with the African church.

faqs.question: Who was Julian of Eclanum?
faqs.answer: He was an Italian bishop who refused to sign Zosimus's condemnation of Pelagianism and was deposed. He became St. Augustine's leading opponent in the later Pelagian debates.
